evidence.claim: Follow a freight canal through industrial cities and surviving canal towns
evidence.quote: The rest of the route follows the Ohio and Erie Canal through cities ranging from large, industrial cities such as Cleveland, Akron, Barberton, and Massillon to small, quaint villages such as Peninsula, Clinton, Navarre, Bolivar, and Zoar.

evidence.claim: a freight canal
evidence.quote: The canal carried freight traffic from 1827 to 1861

evidence.claim: The Ohio & Erie Canalway drive links Cleveland’s neighborhoods and industrial districts with the Cuyahoga Valley and canal towns farther south.
evidence.quote: Between Cleveland and Cuyahoga Valley National Park, the byway is split between three routes.

evidence.claim: The Federal Highway Administration lists this 110-mile route as a National Scenic Byway, allowing four and a half hours for the drive.

evidence.claim: Its description emphasizes working rivers, industrial landscapes and natural areas, with journeys by trail and train as well as road.

evidence.claim: Cleveland’s neighborhoods and industrial districts with the Cuyahoga Valley and canal towns farther south.
evidence.quote: The western route runs through four historic Cleveland neighborhoods: Ohio City, Tremont, Brooklyn Centre, and South Brooklyn. The central route runs through Cleveland's industrial area.

evidence.quote: The Heritage House/Old Canal Days Museum operated by the Canal Fulton Heritage Society exhibits a collection of canal and canal-era memorabilia. A 2½ mile round trip tour on the mule-drawn reproduction canal boat St. Helena III

evidence.claim: The town itself grew from settlements on the Tuscarawas River.
evidence.quote: Canal Fulton traces its history to three villages that developed along the Tuscarawas River.

evidence.claim: Canal construction between 1826 and 1828 brought Fulton into being across the river from Milan.
evidence.quote: Milan was the only village in the township until the building of the canal between 1826 and 1828, which brought about the town of Fulton on the other side of the river.

evidence.claim: Fulton added “Canal” to its name in 1832 and absorbed Milan and West Fulton in 1853.
evidence.quote: Fulton was platted on May 16, 1826, changed its name to Canal Fulton in 1832

evidence.claim: absorbed Milan and West Fulton in 1853.
evidence.quote: In 1853, Canal Fulton absorbed both Milan and West Fulton.

evidence.claim: Digging the canal helped Zoar’s communal society pay for its land.
evidence.quote: The Zoarites then spent several years in the 1820s digging the canal and thus were able to pay off their loans on time with much money to spare.

evidence.claim: German religious dissenters founded the Society of Separatists of Zoar in 1817.
evidence.quote: Zoar was founded by Radical Pietist Christian dissenters from Germany called the Society of Separatists of Zoar in 1817.

evidence.claim: They had bought land sight unseen with loans to repay; when Ohio needed a canal right of way, it offered them paid excavation work.
evidence.quote: The Zoarites had purchased 5,500 acres (22 km2) of land sight unseen and used loans to pay for it.

evidence.claim: That work allowed them to clear the debt on time.
evidence.quote: were able to pay off their loans on time with much money to spare.

evidence.claim: The society dissolved in 1898, dividing its property among the remaining residents.
evidence.quote: By 1898, the village voted to disband the communal society, and the property was divided among the remaining residents.

evidence.claim: Much of the early village layout and many buildings survive.
evidence.quote: Much of the village's early layout survives, as do many buildings from its utopian origins.

evidence.claim: Much of Zoar’s early layout and many buildings from its communal period survive.
evidence.quote: Much of the village's early layout survives, as do many buildings from its utopian origins.

evidence.claim: when Ohio needed a canal right of way, it offered them paid excavation work.
evidence.quote: The state of Ohio required some of the Zoarite land to be used as a right of way and offered the Zoarites an opportunity to assist in digging the canals for money.

evidence.claim: Engineer James Geddes, who had worked on New York’s canals, was hired to design the system.
evidence.quote: James Geddes, an engineer who had worked on the New York canals, was hired.

evidence.quote: the site of the original mills of Ferdinand Schumacher—founder of Quaker Oats; two railroad bridges spanning the gorge

evidence.quote: It now offers a Canalway Visitor Center that provides information, orientation and interpretation products and programs, anchored by tours on the St. Helena III Canal Boat in Canal Fulton

evidence.claim: Elected trustees had managed the society’s farms, shops and factories, with all property held in common.
evidence.quote: All property was communally owned, and the farms, shops, and factories were managed by regularly elected trustees.

flags: The canal article contradicts its own introductory 1861 freight cutoff, describing later boat operations and limited freight after 1913. Replaced the cutoff with decline and continued local use.

The cache documents the canal’s construction, not the modern byway’s road-building or designation campaign. Overview keeps those corridors distinct. Road-surface, curves and grade detail are sparse; use supported landscape and driving-time information.
St. Helena III tours are supported by the ODOT story-map cache, but no dated operator schedule is supplied. Attribute the tour description to ODOT and make no daily-operation or booking promise.

Zoar’s article gives inconsistent land-purchase and repayment chronologies in different sections. Retained the shared account of paid canal work financing the land, omitting acreage, debt totals and a repayment deadline.
